translations: Wu Gang climbed the Immortal Mountain for the first time because he didn’t want to be pushed away by the passing years like ordinary mortals.

He’d seen frail old folks and watched hard‑earned treasures vanish in a single storm, so he decided that if he could master immortal arts, he could dodge all the uncertainties. When he met the immortal master, he spoke earnestly, saying he was ready to endure hardship and start from the very basics.

The master’s first assignment was to fetch water. The spring was far from his hut, so he had to walk back and forth every day, training both mind and breath. After a few days, Wu Gang heard that the eastern peak taught wind‑control, and he instantly thought that if he could ride the wind, he wouldn’t have to walk step by step to draw water.

He set aside the bucket and began learning wind‑control. Halfway through the wind spell, he heard a disciple on the western slope preparing herbs, and he remembered that immortality required celestial plants, so he turned to identify leaves. By evening, he’d memorized half the wind spell and recognized two herbs, but the water bucket was still empty.
The master asked, “What did you learn today?”
Wu Gang replied, “I learned a lot.”
“What did you accomplish?”
He stared at the empty bucket and was at a loss for words.

The master didn’t rush him down the mountain; instead, he told him to keep fetching water the next day. Wu Gang agreed quickly, but on the way he saw fellow disciples stargazing. He thought that mastering wind and herbs required knowing the time, so he left the bucket by a stone and followed the star positions. When he remembered to fetch water, the moon was already up.

Aman, who copied lessons for the immortal sect, saw Wu Gang carrying different scrolls for several days. He wrote on a green bamboo slip: “Wu Gang’s pursuit of immortality isn’t focused; today he studied wind, tomorrow herbs, the next day stargazing. Every path welcomes him, because no one can keep him.”
Wu Gang saw the note and scoffed, “I’m just gathering the best of all.”
Aman asked, “What about the water?”
“I’ll fill it tomorrow for sure.”
“That line is surprisingly focused; I never change it.”

A fellow disciple laughed. Wu Gang laughed too, but didn’t really heed the warning. He still believed he was just mis‑arranging his training; as long as he learned all the mantras together, he’d eventually be faster than someone who focused on just one.

The master gently closed the scroll in his hand, frowned a little, and didn’t lecture further. He simply said, “First fill the bucket, then guard this lamp. Don’t let it go out.” Wu Gang nodded, answered in his mouth, but his eyes sparkled with self‑confidence. He turned and walked toward the courtyard, his steps light as if he were heading to a grand ceremony.

The bucket was heavy, the water reflected the moon palace’s starlight. Wu Gang lifted it with effort, his shoulders aching, yet he muttered to himself, “What’s this? When I master all the mantras at once, even lifting water will become a spell.” He poured the water into a large porcelain basin, splashing, and the droplets landed on the lamp’s wick, making the flame flicker like a tiny smile.

Just as he was about to relight the lamp, Aman quietly approached, holding a bamboo slip, and whispered, “Wu Gang fetched water three times, the lamp trembled once.” Aman looked up at Wu Gang, who had a furrowed brow and was holding the heavy axe, as if he had transferred all the fatigue of fetching water onto the impending cutting of the camphor tree.

Wu Gang raised the axe, his gaze radiating unquestionable confidence: “If I cut the camphor tree in one swing, the penalty will vanish.” He swung the axe hard; the blade sliced the trunk, a crisp sound rang out, bark split, and bright sap rushed out. Yet the tree’s branches trembled gently in the moonlight, and the wound seemed wrapped in a soft ribbon; within seconds the crack closed itself, the bark smoothing back to normal.

Wu Gang froze, his brow furrowed tighter, and muttered, “Why is this tree so stubborn?” Aman lifted his bamboo slip and quickly wrote, “Camphor tree heals after each chop, Wu Gang keeps swinging.” He looked up at Wu Gang, who had already put the axe away, his palm still damp with a few beads of sweat.

“One more time,” Wu Gang whispered, his voice tinged with defiance and impatience. He raised the axe again, faster than before, but still struck once. The bark split, blood sprayed, yet under the moon’s gentle touch the wound was soothed by a soft ribbon and closed instantly.

This time Wu Gang’s brow finally formed a small hill. He looked toward the distant moon palace, where the lamps were sparse and cold, like a forgotten corner. Aman stood nearby, still recording: “Second axe strike, camphor tree still heals.” He lightly tapped his bamboo slip, a barely noticeable smile curling at the corner of his mouth, as if silently mocking the absurd cycle.

Wu Gang’s arm grew sore, the axe felt heavy in his palm, and the impatient flame in his heart slowly cooled under the moon palace’s silence. He whispered to himself, “What am I really chasing? Is it that so‑called great spell, or just a way to escape this endless punishment?”
